title: The Science of Memory and Forgetting
paras: Memory is often compared to a recording device, but scientists now regard it as something far more active. Every time we recall an event, the brain rebuilds it from scattered fragments: a smell here, a face there, a feeling of fear or pleasure. Because this process is a reconstruction rather than a replay, memories can change slightly each time they are used. This helps to explain why two people who witnessed the same accident often describe it in different ways.

Researchers usually divide memory into three stages. First, sensory memory holds an impression of what we see or hear for only a second or two. Information that receives attention then moves into short-term, or working, memory, where an adult can keep about seven items, such as the digits of a telephone number, for roughly half a minute. Only a small part of this material is passed on to long-term memory, which has no known limit and can last for decades.

The transfer depends heavily on how the material is processed. In a well-known type of experiment, volunteers who were asked to think about the meaning of words remembered far more of them than volunteers who simply counted the letters. Linking new facts to things we already know, or creating a vivid mental picture, strengthens the connection. Sleep also plays a part, because the brain appears to replay the day's experiences at night and to store the important ones more securely.

Forgetting, however, is not simply a failure. A nineteenth-century German researcher tested himself on lists of meaningless syllables and found that most of the material vanished within a day, after which the loss slowed down. The resulting forgetting curve has been confirmed many times. It shows that the fastest loss occurs soon after learning, which is why a short review within twenty-four hours is more effective than a long one a week later.

Some forgetting is actually useful. If we remembered every parking space we had ever used, finding today's car would be much harder. Many scientists therefore argue that the brain deliberately allows unimportant details to fade so that valuable information is easier to reach. Others believe that most lost memories are not erased but merely hard to retrieve, because the cues that once pointed to them have disappeared. A familiar song may suddenly bring back a school trip that had been forgotten for years.

Practical studies suggest several ways to improve retention. Spreading study sessions over several days produces better results than cramming in a single night. Testing yourself, instead of rereading notes, forces the brain to retrieve information and makes the memory stronger. Regular exercise and adequate sleep also help, while heavy stress can interfere with the process. No technique makes memory perfect, but understanding how it works allows students to use their time wisely.

title: Growing Food in the City
paras: By 2050 about two out of every three people are expected to live in cities, which raises an old question: where will their food come from? Traditionally, farms have been far from the places where food is eaten, and vegetables have travelled hundreds of kilometres by lorry, ship or plane. Urban farming tries to shorten that journey by growing crops inside the city itself, on rooftops, in empty car parks, in disused buildings and even in shipping containers.

The simplest form is the community garden. Residents of an apartment block rent a small plot on vacant land, or share a roof, and grow tomatoes, herbs and beans for their families. These gardens produce modest harvests, but they bring neighbours together, offer exercise outdoors and teach children where food comes from. In several cities, schools now run their own plots and use the produce in their lunch menus.

More technical methods have appeared in recent years. In hydroponics, plants grow in water containing dissolved nutrients rather than in soil. Vertical farms stack trays of lettuce or herbs in layers inside a warehouse, with LED lamps replacing sunlight. Because the environment is carefully controlled, such farms can harvest many times a year, and they use far less water than open fields, since the water is recycled.

The benefits go beyond fresh produce. Food grown close to consumers needs little transport, so fewer emissions are produced, and it can be picked ripe instead of early. Green roofs also absorb rainwater, which reduces flooding, and they insulate buildings, keeping them cooler in summer. Some projects employ people who have struggled to find work, providing training in horticulture and basic business skills.

Nevertheless, urban farming faces real obstacles. Land in city centres is expensive, and a farm must compete with housing and offices for space. Indoor systems depend on electricity, and the lamps and pumps can cost more to run than the crops are worth unless the energy is cheap or renewable. For this reason, most commercial indoor farms grow only leafy vegetables and herbs, which are light, quick to grow and sell at a good price. Staple foods such as wheat and rice need far too much space to be produced this way.

Experts therefore describe urban farming as a supplement to conventional agriculture, not a replacement for it. It is unlikely to feed a whole city, but it can improve the supply of fresh vegetables, reduce waste and make residents more aware of the food system. Planners increasingly include space for growing in new developments, treating it as part of ordinary urban infrastructure, like parks or cycle lanes. Even a modest roof garden, in this view, is a small step towards a city that depends less on distant farms.

title: A Short History of Maps
paras: Long before written alphabets existed, people drew maps. Scratches on stone and bone, some of them tens of thousands of years old, may show hunting grounds, rivers or camp sites. Early maps were practical tools, made to answer a simple question: how do I reach the place I need? They were not drawn to scale, and they often showed only what mattered to the person who made them.

The first maps that attempted accuracy appeared in ancient civilisations that needed to measure land. In river valleys, floods washed away boundaries every year, so surveyors recorded fields on clay tablets or papyrus so that taxes and ownership could be settled. Greek scholars later added mathematics. They argued that the Earth is a sphere, calculated its size with surprising accuracy, and introduced lines of latitude and longitude, which allowed any place to be described by two numbers.

In medieval Europe, many maps became religious or symbolic. Large circular maps placed a holy city at the centre and filled the edges with imaginary creatures. Their purpose was to express a view of the world rather than to guide travellers. Meanwhile, sailors used a different kind of chart, drawn from experience of coastlines, which showed harbours and straight lines pointing towards the main compass directions. Arab geographers combined travellers' reports with astronomy to produce detailed maps of trade routes across Asia, Africa and Europe.

The age of exploration from the fifteenth century transformed mapmaking. Voyages to new continents brought a flood of information, and the printing press allowed maps to be copied cheaply. In the sixteenth century a new projection was designed that kept compass bearings as straight lines, which made it ideal for navigation. However, it enlarged regions near the poles, so that northern countries looked much bigger than they really were. This distortion still affects how many people imagine the world.

Accuracy improved again when governments began to use triangulation, measuring the angles between distant hills to calculate exact distances. National survey agencies then produced detailed maps of entire countries, which were used for taxes, roads, railways and armies. In the twentieth century aeroplanes and then satellites replaced walking surveyors, since a single photograph taken from the sky could capture an area that would take months to measure on foot.

Today most people use maps on their phones, which rely on satellite signals to show their position in real time. These digital maps combine traffic information, photographs and reviews, and they update constantly. Yet the basic problem has not changed: a flat map can never show a round planet without some distortion. Choosing what to show, and what to leave out, remains a decision made by people, so every map still reflects the priorities of those who draw it.
